title: The prayer at the foundations
hookLine: Ibrahim and Isma'il pray for a messenger from among the people (2:127–129)
carry: pray for the ones not born
tomorrow: What will you worship after me

lines: A FATHER AND SON, LIFTING STONES.
WORDS FOR PEOPLE NOT YET BORN.
cards: Old buildings sometimes have a time capsule sealed into a cornerstone: a newspaper, a few coins, a letter to whoever opens it in a hundred years. The builders will never meet that reader. They write anyway.
In al-Baqarah, a father and son are raising the foundations of a house in a dry valley in Arabia. As they lift the stones, they speak, and much of what they say is for people who don't exist yet.
Today: the prayer at the foundations.

teach.b: Last year you watched Ibrahim and Isma'il raise the Kaaba. This year, listen to what they said while they did it.
Verse one hundred twenty-seven, in Pickthall's words: “Our Lord! Accept from us (this duty). Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Hearer, the Knower.”
They're building God's house, and their first words ask that it be accepted, as if it might not be. Then the prayer grows.
Make us both submissive to You, and from our descendants a nation submissive to You. Show us our rites, and turn to us.

Then, in verse one hundred twenty-nine, the furthest request: Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves, who will recite Your verses to them, teach them the book and wisdom, and purify them.
Muslims hold that it was answered long after, in the same valley, in Mecca, with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

teach.h: I AM THE ANSWER TO IBRAHIM'S PRAYER
teach.b: A report in the Musnad of Ahmad has him say: I am the answer to the prayer of my father Ibrahim, and the good news of Isa. Notice the order inside the prayer. Accept what we did.
Make us good. Make our children good. Send them a teacher.
It moves outward, from the two of them to people they'd never see. The stones they lifted can't be pointed to today. The prayer is still read, in this surah, every day.

how: Muslims often recite Ibrahim and Isma'il's words, Rabbana taqabbal minna, our Lord, accept from us, after completing a good deed, and pray for their children and for generations to come.

o: the house Ibrahim and Isma'il raised in Mecca
a black stone set into a wall in Jerusalem
the tent where Ibrahim welcomed the angels

games.q: the builders' prayer — tap the pairs.
p: make us and our descendants submissive
I am the answer to Ibrahim's prayer

s: Ibrahim and Isma'il asked for nothing while they built
they prayed the whole time: acceptance, good descendants, a messenger.
Muslims hold that the prayer for a messenger was answered in the same valley
in Mecca, with the Prophet Muhammad.

games.q: you and your son have just raised the foundations of God's house. what are your first words?
games.why: accept from us: they ask for acceptance, as if the work might not be enough, then pray outward to their descendants.

practice: Hold in mind people you'll never meet, or barely will: grandchildren, your students' students, whoever lives in your home after you, a child born this year far away.
If you pray, use the builders' first words, Our Lord, accept from us, and then ask good for them in your own words; if you don't, simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Kaaba. The house Ibrahim and Isma'il raised in Mecca, praying as they built it for descendants and a messenger not yet born. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: our Lord, accept from us; the builders' first words in 2:127.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for the ones not born. The builders at the Kaaba did. See you tomorrow.
